Search words and phrases, then inspect their distribution

Source: vignettes/concordance-and-dispersion.Rmd
concordance-and-dispersion.Rmd

Three occurrences can be spread through a document or concentrated near its beginning. A frequency table alone does not show that difference. This guide first finds words or phrases in their original contexts, then uses the same saved occurrences for context sorting, position plots and a within-document dispersion measure. It keeps the search unit, excluded positions and denominators visible so that a changed search can be explained.

Use ldfreq 0.3.0.9009 or later and optional quanteda >= 4.5.0; plotting also needs ggplot2. Install these packages before running the guide. The four helpers live in examples/concordance.R and are explicitly sourced, installed example code. They are not exported package functions. The example inputs and lemmas are authored for hand checking; they are not learner observations or an evaluation of an annotation system.

Prepare complete annotations 

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "concordance-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
annotations <- demo$annotations
knitr::kable(annotations$segments[c("document_id", "segment_id", "text")], row.names = FALSE)
document_id segment_id text
spread s1 learn a b c learn d e f learn g h i
cluster s1 learn learn learn a b c d e f g h i
context s1 We learn new words. They learned new words.
context s2 learn very new words
absent s1 read a book
empty s1

spread and cluster each contain 12 original tokens and three instances of learn, at positions 1/5/9 and 1/2/3 respectively. context has two segments and includes learned; absent has no matching word and empty has no tokens.

For your own data, supply an unchanged lexdiv_import_annotations() result:

Input Required information
tokens One row per original token: document_id, segment_id, consecutive token_index, original surface; optional character fields such as lemma
segments Document and segment IDs plus original text, in the intended document order; include an empty segment for an empty document
provenance Language, analyzer/version, dictionary/version, unit and normalization declarations

The importer checks complete surface alignment and supplies segment-local character spans. Import before excluding punctuation or other tokens. Only whitespace may fall between supplied surfaces. The search rejects modified import results: edit the original input and import it again. A filtered lexical token vector is not a complete annotation table. See external annotations for analyzer recipes and annotated corpora for the existing corpus adapters. No analyzer or dictionary is downloaded by this guide.

For a short English text without supplied annotations, the following explicit quanteda tokenization recipe can prepare complete surfaces. The alignment check will reject text that this tokenizer changes or leaves partly uncovered; inspect the tokens and adjust the chosen annotation route, rather than dropping the check. Declare sentence/turn segments first if matches must respect them.

raw_segments <- data.frame(document_id = c("my_text", "empty"),
  segment_id = "s1", text = c("We learn new words. We learned them.", ""))
raw_tokens <- as.list(quanteda::tokens(raw_segments$text, what = "word",
  remove_punct = FALSE, remove_symbols = FALSE, remove_numbers = FALSE,
  remove_url = FALSE, remove_separators = TRUE, split_hyphens = FALSE))
raw_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(raw_tokens), function(i) data.frame(
  document_id = rep(raw_segments$document_id[i], length(raw_tokens[[i]])),
  segment_id = rep(raw_segments$segment_id[i], length(raw_tokens[[i]])),
  token_index = seq_along(raw_tokens[[i]]), surface = raw_tokens[[i]])))
raw_annotations <- lexdiv_import_annotations(raw_rows, raw_segments,
  list(language = "en", analyzer = "quanteda-tokens-word",
    analyzer_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("quanteda")),
    dictionary = "none", dictionary_version = "not-applicable",
    unit = "word-tokenizer-with-punctuation", normalization = "none",
    settings = paste("remove_punct=FALSE; remove_symbols=FALSE; remove_numbers=FALSE;",
      "remove_url=FALSE; remove_separators=TRUE; split_hyphens=FALSE")))
raw_search <- helper$concordance_search(raw_annotations,
  list(learning = "^learn(ed)?$"), valuetype = "regex")
raw_search$counts
#>   document_id query_id occurrences
#> 1     my_text learning           2
#> 2       empty learning           0

This recipe preserves punctuation as original positions and adds no lemmas. It treats each row as one searchable segment, so it does not impose sentence boundaries within that row. Save the original texts and tokenizer settings.

Choose a search unit and pattern 

keep <- !annotations$tokens$surface %in% c(".", "very")
search <- helper$concordance_search(annotations,
  queries = list(word = "learn", phrase = c("learn", "new"), absent = "unlisted"),
  term_col = "lemma", valuetype = "fixed", case_insensitive = FALSE,
  keep = keep, window = 2L)
knitr::kable(search$counts, row.names = FALSE)
document_id query_id occurrences
spread word 3
cluster word 3
context word 3
absent word 0
empty word 0
spread phrase 0
cluster phrase 0
context phrase 2
absent phrase 0
empty phrase 0
spread absent 0
cluster absent 0
context absent 0
absent absent 0
empty absent 0 
knitr::kable(search$occurrences[c("query_id", "document_id", "segment_id",
  "pre", "keyword", "post")], row.names = FALSE)
query_id document_id segment_id pre keyword post
word spread s1 learn a b
word spread s1 b c learn d e
word spread s1 e f learn g h
word cluster s1 learn learn learn
word cluster s1 learn learn learn a
word cluster s1 learn learn learn a b
word context s1 We learn new words
word context s1 . They learned new words
word context s2 learn very new
phrase context s1 We learn new words.
phrase context s1 . They learned new words.

Each named list element is one query ID. A character vector within it specifies consecutive token patterns: c("learn", "new") searches two tokens, while "learn new" is one literal token pattern and is not split automatically. term_col selects the supplied surface, lemma or another character annotation. The displayed keyword and context always come from the original surface text. Thus the lemma query learn finds both learn and learned here.

Matching follows quanteda’s pattern rules and value types:

valuetype Example Meaning
"fixed" "learn" Literal token matching with the declared case policy
"glob" "learn*" * matches zero or more characters; ? matches one
"regex" "^learn(ed)?$" A regular expression applied to each token; anchors restrict it to a whole token 
wildcard <- helper$concordance_search(annotations,
  list(forms = "learn*", phrase = c("learn*", "new")), valuetype = "glob", keep = keep)
regular <- helper$concordance_search(annotations,
  list(forms = "^learn(ed)?$"), valuetype = "regex", keep = keep)
knitr::kable(wildcard$counts, row.names = FALSE)
document_id query_id occurrences
spread forms 3
cluster forms 3
context forms 3
absent forms 0
empty forms 0
spread phrase 0
cluster phrase 0
context phrase 2
absent phrase 0
empty phrase 0 
stopifnot(sum(regular$counts$occurrences) == 9L)

Regex is applied to tokens, not to the raw text. An unanchored learn regex also matches unlearn. Fixed matching is not a byte-identity check: quanteda may match canonically equivalent Unicode spellings. Original surface strings and character spans remain unchanged, and quanteda/stringi/ICU versions are saved. The existing exact phrase-review recipe uses its own stricter surface comparison; its decisions and counts are unchanged.

Every contiguous match is retained, including overlapping phrases and identical patterns under different query IDs. Do not sum different query counts as a unique-token coverage measure. Matches and context stop at supplied segment boundaries; sentence boundaries apply only when represented as segments. Excluded tokens and missing/blank search terms leave gaps and cannot complete a phrase, including a wildcard phrase. The example therefore does not turn learn very new into learn new after excluding very.

knitr::kable(search$documents, row.names = FALSE)
document_id source_tokens kept_tokens searchable_tokens missing_terms
spread 12 12 12 0
cluster 12 12 12 0
context 14 11 11 0
absent 3 3 3 0
empty 0 0 0 0

source_tokens counts all original positions. kept_tokens applies keep; searchable_tokens also requires a nonblank search term. missing_terms counts kept positions with no usable term. None of these choices renumbers positions. The context window counts original positions, so excluded punctuation can still appear as context. The default max_cells = 1e6 limits original token slots, document-query count cells and the match/context allocation separately; it is not a memory-size guarantee. Reduce the saved window or split intended searches before raising it for a larger input.

Sort by the nearest context words 

right_sorted <- helper$concordance_sort(search, side = "right", depth = 2L)
left_sorted <- helper$concordance_sort(search, side = "left", depth = 2L)
knitr::kable(right_sorted[c("query_id", "document_id", "pre", "keyword", "post")], row.names = FALSE)
query_id document_id pre keyword post
word spread learn a b
word cluster learn learn learn a b
word spread b c learn d e
word spread e f learn g h
word cluster learn learn learn a
word cluster learn learn learn
word context We learn new words
word context . They learned new words
word context learn very new
phrase context We learn new words.
phrase context . They learned new words.

The saved left_tokens and right_tokens list columns start with the nearest surface token. Left sorting uses L1, then L2; right sorting uses R1, then R2. It does not alphabetize the complete displayed pre string. Ties retain query order, supplied segment order and original match position. Absent context sorts last at each depth. Sorting uses UTF-8 radix order, independent of locale, rather than language-specific collation. ignore_case = TRUE case-folds only the sort keys. Request a depth no larger than the saved window.

from/to are segment token positions. document_from/document_to concatenate original segment slots in supplied order, without inventing separator tokens. start/end are 1-based, inclusive Unicode-codepoint positions within the original segment, not byte offsets or positions in a newly joined text. occurrence_id identifies a match within the saved search condition. Changing queries, settings or source creates a different search identity; sorting does not.

Plot those same occurrences 

positions <- helper$concordance_positions(search, "word")
positions

Each plus marks the original start position. A horizontal stroke also shows the matched span for a multi-token query. Document labels retain match and original token counts, including zero-match and empty documents. An empty document has no occurrence or text-length line. This is an occurrence plot, not a density estimate or a dispersion statistic.

Relative coordinates are (position - 0.5) / source_tokens, the centers of the original token slots on a common 0–1 scale. Exclusions do not shorten the axis. Use relative = FALSE for a shared absolute token-position axis:

helper$concordance_positions(search, "phrase", relative = FALSE, monochrome = TRUE)

stopifnot(identical(positions$data$occurrence_id,
  search$occurrences$occurrence_id[search$occurrences$query_id == "word"]))

The plot reads the saved table without retokenization or a new search. Its data retains occurrence IDs and coordinates for inspection. Colour is the default; monochrome = TRUE keeps the same marks and axes. Add figure numbering, titles and explanatory notes in the surrounding manuscript.

Calculate within-document DP

This recipe implements the unnormalized DP definition in Gries (2008, Section 3):

DP=12∑j=1K|oj−sj|,oj=fj/∑jfj,sj=nj/∑jnj. DP = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{K}|o_j-s_j|, \qquad o_j=f_j/\sum_j f_j,\quad s_j=n_j/\sum_j n_j.

Here parts = K divides each document’s original token slots into fixed intervals, with part index floor((position - 1) * K / N) + 1 for original length N. Within each part, f_j counts saved matches and n_j counts searchable tokens. Exclusions and missing terms can make these exposure counts unequal. The result retains original interval bounds, both counts and both shares. A larger value indicates greater departure from the declared exposure distribution; it does not necessarily mean a geometrically narrower cluster.

dispersion <- helper$concordance_dispersion(search, "word", parts = 3L)
knitr::kable(dispersion$documents[c("document_id", "searchable_tokens", "occurrences",
  "DP", "status", "missing_reason")], digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
document_id searchable_tokens occurrences DP status missing_reason
spread 12 3 0.0000 ok NA
cluster 12 3 0.6667 ok NA
context 11 3 0.0606 ok NA
absent 3 0 NA missing no_matches
empty 0 0 NA missing no_searchable_tokens 
knitr::kable(subset(dispersion$parts, document_id %in% c("spread", "cluster"))[
  c("document_id", "part", "searchable_tokens", "occurrences", "expected_share", "observed_share")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
document_id part searchable_tokens occurrences expected_share observed_share
spread 1 4 1 0.333 0.333
spread 2 4 1 0.333 0.333
spread 3 4 1 0.333 0.333
cluster 1 4 3 0.333 1.000
cluster 2 4 0 0.333 0.000
cluster 3 4 0 0.333 0.000 
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(dispersion$documents$DP[1:2], c(0, 2/3))))

For spread, all three parts contain four searchable tokens and one match: both shares are (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), so DP is 0. For cluster, the match shares are (1, 0, 0) with the same exposure shares, so DP is (|1 - 1/3| + |0 - 1/3| + |0 - 1/3|) / 2 = 2/3.

This is within-document, single-token-query DP, including a regex/glob that selects a class of individual tokens. It does not compare the distribution across documents. Multi-token queries are rejected for DP because they require a separately defined phrase-opportunity denominator; their position plots remain available. No small-sample, maximum-value or frequency correction is applied. Total concentration in a part with exposure share s gives 1 - s, not necessarily 1. DP depends on frequency and partition choice; it is neither a significance test nor a proficiency measure.

No searchable tokens or no matches yield NA with a distinct missing_reason. The recipe also requires at least two parts with positive searchable exposure; otherwise it returns fewer_than_two_nonempty_parts. A single match is computable when that requirement is met, but its value largely reflects which part contains it. These missing-value rules and the partition are explicit choices of this recipe. Report frequency, counts, boundaries and exclusions beside DP; do not compare different query or partition policies silently.

Save and reopen the complete analysis 

record <- list(search = search, sorted = right_sorted, dispersion = dispersion,
  sort = list(side = "right", depth = 2L, ignore_case = FALSE),
  session = utils::sessionInfo())
saved <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") # Choose a persistent filename for research data.
saveRDS(record, saved)
restored <- readRDS(saved)
stopifnot(identical(restored, record),
  identical(helper$concordance_sort(restored$search, "right", 2L), restored$sorted),
  identical(helper$concordance_dispersion(restored$search, "word", 3L), restored$dispersion),
  identical(restored$dispersion$occurrence_ids,
    restored$search$occurrences$occurrence_id[restored$search$occurrences$query_id == "word"]))
unlink(saved)

In a fresh R session, source examples/concordance.R and read the RDS before calling these helpers. The saved search includes complete source annotations, queries, selection masks, versions, counts and occurrence IDs. Integrity checks reject edited saved results; rerun the search from newly imported source when changing an input. These hashes check accidental changes, not authorship. A flattened CSV cannot retain the source object, settings and context-vector columns; use it only as a display or exchange table beside the complete RDS.

To connect documents to writers, tasks and occasions, join their retained document_id to your explicit metadata map; see the repeated-observation guide. KWIC rows and overlapping matches are not independent participants. This guide checks search and calculation behavior; it does not establish an inferential model or validate a language-learning outcome.

Gries, S. Th. (2008). Dispersions and adjusted frequencies in corpora. International Journal of Corpus Linguistics, 13(4), 403–437. https://doi.org/10.1075/ijcl.13.4.02gri
